paper_title: Unlocking the Power of Loops in Pretrained LLMs with Loop Residuals

sections.title: Abstract
sections.content: Looped Transformers iterate a shared block of layers to increase computation without adding parameters, offering stronger performance and test-time scaling. However, this power has so far required training from scratch and yielded only modest gains for LLMs. Finetuning existing models into loops is far cheaper, yet also brings only marginal gains over SFT. We propose LoopRes, an effective, scalable, and simple approach that turns loops into significant and consistent gains for pretrained LLMs. Building on Attention Residuals, LoopRes lets each looped layer attend directly to the outputs of earlier loops. Since these outputs are iterates of the same layers and become harder to tell apart, we give each a trainable loop-aware key that encodes its structural identity. Attending to all earlier loops also lets layers skip intermediate ones, so we restrict each layer to a residual window of the latest W loops, forcing every loop to build incrementally on recent ones. Across 6 pretrained LLMs from 3 model families and 9 benchmarks, LoopRes delivers significant and consistent gains: at 2x compute, it improves Qwen3-1.7B-Base by 29.1% over SFT, more than doubling the gain of the state-of-the-art baseline. The gains hold on larger models up to 30B and across all three families. More importantly, from 1.7B to 8B, LoopRes scales more steeply than SFT as compute grows, reaching a higher ceiling while needing less compute on long outputs. These results establish LoopRes as an effective looping approach, delivering both better performance and better test-time scaling.

Across 6 pretrained LLMs from 3 model families and 9 benchmarks, LoopRes delivers significant and consistent gains: at 2 compute, it improves Qwen3-1.7B-Base by 29.1% over SFT, more than doubling the gain of the state-of-the-art baseline. More importantly, from 1.7B to 8B, LoopRes scales more steeply than SFT as compute grows, reaching higher ceiling while needing less compute on long outputs. These results establish LoopRes as an effective looping approach, delivering both better performance and better test-time scaling. 1. Introduction Looped Transformers reuse shared block of layers multiple times in single forward pass, achieving deeper computation without adding parameters (Dehghani et al., 2019; Giannou et al., 2023). Depth scales with the number of loops rather than the number of layers, making loops Unlocking the Power of Loops in Pretrained LLMs with Loop Residuals Figure 2. How looped layer takes the outputs of earlier layers as input. Each panel diagrams three layers running for up to three loops, highlighting one layers input, where ℓ(t) denotes layer of loop and dashed layers have not yet run. Loops before t2 are omitted in (c) and (d). (a) layer loop iterates each layer through every loop, passing only the previous iteration forward. (b) stack loop feeds only the last layer of each loop into the first of the next. (c) AttnRes attends to every earlier loop output with content-based weights. (d) LoopRes attends only to window of the latest loops (shaded, =1 here) and adds loop-aware key alongside the content key. Each bar marks the magnitude of score term. simple lever for both stronger performance and test-time compute scaling. Yet turning this promise into significant and consistent gains for LLMs remains an open challenge. One line of work pretrains looped LLMs from scratch (Geiping et al., 2025; Zhu et al., 2025). However, the gains remain modest or even negative at comparable cost (Zeitoun et al., 2026; Wang et al., 2026). Given the expense of pretraining, this direction offers limited returns. more promising approach finetunes pretrained LLMs into loops (Marchenko et al., 2026; You et al., 2026), reusing their learned capabilities at fraction of the pretraining cost. As illustrated in Figure 2a,b, although these designs vary in their looping pattern (Zhu et al., 2025; You et al., 2026; Geiping et al., 2025; Zeitoun et al., 2026; Wang et al., 2026; Zhuang et al., 2026; Marques et al., 2026), they all compress the outputs of earlier loops into narrow pathway. This limits what later loops can build on, yielding only marginal gains and leaving the potential of loops largely unrealized. natural remedy is to let each looped layer attend directly to the outputs of earlier loops. Attention Residuals (AttnRes) (Kimi Team et al., 2026) offer exactly this: each layer builds its input by attending to all earlier layer outputs. However, AttnRes is designed for standard Transformers, where the sources differ in content and are fixed in number. Our key insight is that loops break both assumptions: the sources are iterates of the same layers, so they become similar in content and grow in number. This causes three problems. (i) Similar iterates. The outputs are iterates of the same layers and grow harder to tell apart as loops deepen. (ii) Early convergence. The AttnRes weights converge early in finetuning, and because the keys come from similar outputs, the model cannot learn to tell sources apart before the pattern is set. (iii) Growing sources. Each loop adds new sources to the full attention window, so layers can shortcut to earlier loops, skipping intermediate ones. Based on these observations, we propose Loop Residuals (LoopRes), an effective, scalable, and simple approach that turns loops into significant and consistent gains for pretrained LLMs. LoopRes builds on AttnRes and introduces two improvements. (i) It assigns each source trainable, loop-aware key alongside its content key, encoding the structural relationship of loops and layers. Because these keys are directly optimized, the model can learn to differentiate sources before the weights converge. (ii) It restricts each layer to residual window of the latest loops. This eliminates shortcuts to earlier loops, forces every loop to build incrementally on recent ones, and keeps the overhead constant as loops deepen. Across 6 pretrained LLMs from 3 model families and 9 math and code benchmarks, LoopRes delivers significant and consistent gains. On Qwen3-1.7B-Base at 2 compute, it improves the average score by 29.1% over SFT, more than doubling the gain of the SOTA baseline, and its gain continues to grow as loops deepen. The gains are consistent: LoopRes improves by 10.0% to 37.7% on the larger Qwen3- {4B,8B,30B-A3B}-Base, as well as on Qwen3.5 and Llama3.2 from different families. Notably, LoopRes on the 4B backbone even surpasses SFT on the 8B one, showing that loops can bridge the gap to larger models. More importantly, LoopRes achieves better scaling at test time: from 1.7B to 8B, its score rises with steeper slope than SFT as compute grows. It thus reaches higher ceiling, significantly exceeding the best score of SFT. At the same time, it is more efficient on long outputs, reaching the same score at lower compute cost. Together, these results establish loop depth as an axis of test-time scaling, benefiting both inference and post-training rollouts. As shown in Figure 3a, the iterates of the same block are far more similar to each other than to other blocks. Because the content keys are derived from these Unlocking the Power of Loops in Pretrained LLMs with Loop Residuals sources, similar iterates receive similar scores. With three loops, the output query in Figure 3b clearly separates the two blocks, but the iterates within each block are hard to tell apart. With seven loops in Figure 3d, this worsens, as many iterates collapse onto nearly the same score. Early convergence. As shown in Figure 3c, the query norm reaches most of its final value within the first third of finetuning and then levels off. We hypothesize that this commits the model to its early connection pattern, since content keys change only indirectly, through the hidden states. Growing sources. The source set grows with every loop, and AttnRes attends to all of them, so layers can skip intermediate loops. As shown in Figure 3e, the weight on the path through every loop falls from 33.7% with three loops to 0.05% with seven loops, and the most likely paths never reach the later loops, suggesting that deeper loops add little effective depth. 2.4. LoopRes Building on the analysis above, we propose LoopRes, an effective, scalable, and simple approach that turns loops into significant and consistent gains for pretrained LLMs. As illustrated in Figure 2d, LoopRes keeps the input-dependent mechanism of AttnRes and introduces two improvements: (i) It assigns each source loop-aware key alongside its content key, which resolves the identity of each iterate. (ii) It restricts each layer to residual window of the previous loops, which bounds the number of sources as the loop deepens. Figure 9 provides PyTorch-style pseudo code. Loop-aware keys. (ii) It is optimized directly, so the connection pattern no longer adapts only through the hidden states. Residual window. LoopRes restricts the residual sources to window of the previous loops. This brings three benefits: (i) It prevents layers from skipping to distant loops, forcing each loop to build on the latest loops. (ii) It keeps the softmax from shrinking the weight of the current loop as sources accumulate. (iii) It bounds each input to (W + 1)B + 1 sources, thus limiting compute, memory, and communication overhead to loops. Efficiency. naive implementation of Equation 3 loads all queries and keys, then writes the weighted sum for every sub-layer. Following the design of FlashAttention (Dao, 2024), we fuse these steps into single Triton (Tillet et al., 2019) kernel that loads each source once from HBM and writes only the result back, significantly reducing IO cost and peak memory. 3. Either key alone performs worse than the two combined at both compute budgets. As loops deepen, dropping the loop-aware key hurts more, while using it alone approaches LoopRes. This is likely because iterates become harder to tell apart by content as loops deepen, making structural information more important. 3.5. Analysis What LoopRes learns. We visualize how LoopRes weighs its sources, revealing three patterns. Iterative loop updates. In Figure 7a,b, each layer balances its input across the prelude, the loop outputs, and the partial sum. Within the loop outputs, the first block mainly updates its own output from the previous loop, with small share from the other block of that loop. The second block on average relies most on the first block of the current loop, indicating that LoopRes learns the iterative structure of the loop. Dominant loop-aware keys. In Figure 7c, the loop-aware key accounts for most of the selection at both compute budgets, with the content key taking smaller share. Adaptive content keys. Despite its smaller share, the content key lets each token choose its own depth. In Figure 7d, simple tokens such as But and Wait favor shallower outputs, while difficult tokens such as digits and math symbols favor deeper ones. This suggests that the content key recognizes the difficulty of each token and allocates computation accordingly. How LoopRes differs from AttnRes. We further compare LoopRes with AttnRes, with and without the residual window, revealing three differences. Distinguishable loop iterates. In Figure 8a, AttnRes struggles to tell adjacent loops apart even with the window, while LoopRes separates them clearly from early in finetuning. Recency-focused inputs. In Figure 8b, the last block of AttnRes gives sizable share of its weight to the first loop. The window removes these shortcuts, and LoopRes further concentrates the weight on the preceding block. Less is more for content keys. In Figure 8c,d, the content score of AttnRes is almost fixed preference over sources and barely varies with the token. Although the content key takes smaller share in LoopRes, its score varies far more with the token, even as loops deepen, likely because the loop-aware key takes over the fixed preference. 7 Unlocking the Power of Loops in Pretrained LLMs with Loop Residuals 4. Related Work Residual connections. Residual connections (He et al., 2016) add each layers output to shared stream with fixed unit weights and remain standard in modern LLMs. DenseNet (Huang et al., 2017) instead feeds each layer the outputs of all preceding layers. mHC (Xie et al., 2025) expands the residual stream into parallel streams and constrains their mixing to preserve the identity mapping. AttnRes (Kimi Team et al., 2026) replaces the fixed accumulation with softmax attention over preceding layer outputs, allowing each layer to aggregate them with learned, input-dependent weights. However, these designs target non-looped networks, where the sources differ in content and are fixed in number. LoopRes is instead designed for loops, where the sources are iterates of the same layers and grow with the loop count. Layer loops. Layer loops repeat layer or block of consecutive layers before advancing to the next. Sequence sharing (Takase & Kiyono, 2023) ties adjacent layers, so that each unique layer runs several times in row. BRT (Marques et al., 2026) extends this to blocks, partitioning the layers into contiguous blocks and recursively reusing each block before moving to the next. However, both keep the standard residual stream and learn no connections across loops. Stack loops. Stack loops repeat all layers or contiguous subset end to end. Universal Transformers (Dehghani et al., 2019) apply shared transition recurrently with dynamic halting mechanism, and looped Transformers have since been shown to emulate programmable computers (Giannou et al., 2023) and to nearly match deeper non-looped models on synthetic reasoning tasks (Saunshi et al., 2025). Direct looping feeds each loop the output of the previous loop. WideNet (Xue et al., 2022) shares attention and mixture-of-experts layers across blocks with individual layer normalization, Ouro (Zhu et al., 2025) loops the full stack with learned early exit for adaptive computation, and TaH (Fu et al., 2026) feeds back logit-weighted embeddings for the tokens selected by neural decider, with duo-causal attention over the key-value states of earlier loops. Input injection additionally feeds the input into each loop. Huginn (Geiping et al., 2025) joins the latent state and the input embedding through linear adapter, Parcae (Prairie et al., 2026) constrains the spectral norm of the injection parameters for stability, CloseLoop (Marchenko et al., 2026) mixes the token embedding into each later loop with one learned scalar, and TaH2 (You et al., 2026) extends TaH with an injection updater and an iteration decider that focuses extra iterations on the tokens that benefit. Cross-loop aggregation combines the states of multiple 8 loops. Hyperloop (Zeitoun et al., 2026) maintains parallel residual streams and mixes them with hyper-connections after each loop, WMRE (Zhuang et al., 2026) conditions each loop on its differences from recent states, and InfiLoop (Li et al., 2026) keeps running summary of earlier outputs with content-based weights and learned temporal decay. Nevertheless, the input of each loop in these designs remains one or few states compressed from earlier loops. Different from them, LoopRes keeps each block output as separate source and lets every sub-layer build its input by attending directly to the sources of the latest loops, with loopaware key that tells the iterates apart. 5. Conclusion In this work, we presented LoopRes, an effective, scalable, and simple approach that lets each looped layer attend directly to the outputs of earlier loops. LoopRes assigns each source trainable loop-aware key that encodes the structural relationship of loops and layers, and restricts each layer to residual window of the latest loops so that every loop builds incrementally on recent ones. Across 6 pretrained LLMs from 3 model families and 9 math and code benchmarks, LoopRes delivered significant and consistent gains, more than doubling the improvement of the strongest compute. Its score rose with steeper slope baseline at 2 than SFT as compute grew, reaching higher ceiling and needing less compute to match SFT on long outputs. As illustrated in ??, these advantages benefit both inference and post-training rollouts. We hope LoopRes serves as simple and effective foundation for scaling LLMs along the loop-depth axis. Limitations. Our experiments cover math and code benchmarks, and the gains on broader tasks such as general instruction following and open-ended generation remain to be validated. Additionally, LoopRes has been evaluated with supervised finetuning only, and its interaction with reinforcement learning has not yet been explored. Future work. One key direction is to combine LoopRes with reinforcement learning, where the lower cost of matching SFT on long outputs could reduce the rollout budget. Another direction is to explore adaptive loop depth, allowing the model to decide how many loops each token or sequence needs. Furthermore, our findings suggest that the loop-depth scaling curve has not yet saturated on larger backbones, motivating further study of looping at greater scale. Finally, our analysis reveals that the learned loop dependencies follow clear, structured patterns, suggesting that simpler, fixed connection scheme may capture most of the benefit without the overhead of learned attention weights. Unlocking the Power of Loops in Pretrained LLMs with Loop Residuals

sections.title: Impact Statement
sections.content: LoopRes improves the math and code performance of pretrained LLMs by finetuning them into loops, rather than pretraining larger models from scratch. This may lower the cost of obtaining capable models and broaden access for researchers and practitioners. However, stronger reasoning and coding capabilities may also be misused, for example to generate malicious code. We therefore encourage safety evaluations and safeguards before deployment. Finally, looping increases the computation per token, which may raise energy consumption at scale.

Baselines We reimplement every baseline on the same backbone and train it with its own objective, the cross-entropy of the last loop unless stated otherwise. Since two of them are unnamed, we call them WMRE (Zhuang et al., 2026) and CloseLoop (Marchenko et al., 2026) after their titles. The originals of Ouro, InfiLoop, BRT, Huginn, Hyperloop, and WMRE pretrain from scratch; we finetune the pretrained backbone throughout. Every token runs all loops, in training and at inference, and the three core-looped designs run the coda once, on the last loops output. Ouro (Zhu et al., 2025). Our implementation loops all layers, each loop reading the previous loops normed output, and averages the cross-entropy over all loops. The original weights the loops by learned exit distribution under an entropy-regularized objective; we remove the exit gate and weight the loops uniformly. TaH2-fixed (You et al., 2026). The papers fixed-depth variant, following its released recipe. It keeps TaH2s updater, SwiGLU block as wide as the model that merges the token embeddings with the previous loops output, and removes the iteration decider. Attention runs in the released codes causal mode: earlier tokens expose their loop-1 keys, and each token reads its own keys of the later loops. The model predicts from the mean of the loops next-token distributions, and the objective is the cross-entropy of this mean. CloseLoop (Marchenko et al., 2026). Loop > 1 reads we + (1 w)ht1, with the sigmoid of one trained scalar at the papers = 0.99, and the LM head is untied, starting as copy of the input embeddings. An exit gate scores each loop, and the objective weights the loops cross-entropy by the exit distribution, with the papers smoothing 0.05 and entropy coefficient 0.15. We omit the papers optional loop-specific LoRA adapters and always predict from loop L. InfiLoop (Li et al., 2026). Each loop reads running average of the earlier loops outputs, weighted by trained decay and content score, exp(wRMSNorm(zt)) clamped to [ 8, 8], with the released codes initialization (w at zero, the decay at 0.55). The original runs two-level recurrence with one average per level, restarts the inner one each cycle, seeds the outer one with learned state, and backpropagates only through the last cycle; we keep single average over the loops, seed it with the token embeddings, and backpropagate through all of them. Its post-norm layers also keep the averaged states at unit scale, while we average the raw residual stream of the pre-norm backbone. BRT (Marques et al., 2026). Consecutive layers are grouped into blocks, and each block runs times on the standard residual stream before the next. We use seven blocks of four layers on the 28-layer backbone, where the original defaults to two blocks. Huginn (Geiping et al., 2025). Retrofitted with the same prelude, core, and coda as LoopRes: each loop the core reads Parcaes diagonal injection (Prairie et al., 2026) of the previous core output and the prelude output, initialized at its retention 1/5 with the injection the identity, so that one loop reproduces the pretrained model. The original samples the loop count from log-normal Poisson distribution, draws the initial state from truncated normal, and joins the two inputs by linear (cid:112) map of their concatenation; we fix the loop count, start the state at zero, and use the diagonal adapter. Hyperloop (Zeitoun et al., 2026). The core runs on four parallel residual streams, joined after each loop by its own sigmoid-gated hyper-connection, with per-loop vector trained from zero added to the core output, and the coda reads the stream mean. The gate scales start at mHCs 0.01 (Xie et al., 2025), and the biases start the pre, post, and res gates at 1/4, 1, and 1/2. The stream count and the beginmiddleend split match the original. WMRE (Zhuang et al., 2026). The papers H+LG configuration, on the same split as LoopRes: ht + gate over the papers eight time features scales each loops update. Both sets of weights train from zero. loop + 1 reads 2 that reach back to the first loop, with ht the state after loop t, and scalar ht) over the lags (htj bj (cid:80) A.3.
